items.desc: Functiebeschrijving Every day, radiologists review hundreds of scans to find out whether a patient has cancer. The number of scans keeps growing, but the number of radiologists does not. AI can help. For prostate cancer, AI systems can now read MRI scans about as well as experienced radiologists. Yet today a radiologist still checks every scan, so the AI saves little time. That could change if AI were allowed to handle the clear-cut cases on its own, leaving radiologists more time for the difficult ones. But a hospital is not a static environment. European law now requires hospitals and manufacturers to keep monitoring AI once it is in use, but nobody has yet shown how to do that reliably in practice. items.desc: Job Description Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is an inherited retinal disease that progressively damages photoreceptors, the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision. Although new treatments, including gene therapies, are emerging, monitoring disease progression remains challenging because current clinical imaging techniques cannot always detect subtle changes in these cells. Adaptive optics imaging enables visualisation of individual cone photoreceptors in the living human eye. However, in patients with RP, these cells often appear irregular, with changes in their shape, reflectivity, and […] tial organisation. This makes automated detection and quantification difficult, while the relationship between these abnormalities and visual function is not yet fully understood. Within the AICON project, Erasmus MC and the Rotterdam Eye Hospital aim to address these challenges by developing AI-based methods to automatically detect, quantify, and characterise cone photoreceptors in patients with RP. By combining adaptive optics imaging with Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) and microperimetry, the project will investigate how microscopic changes relate to retinal structure, visual function, and disease progression. The ultimate goal is to develop reliable imaging biomarkers to support disease monitoring and future clinical trials. As a PhD candidate, you will play a central role in this project, developing and validating AI and image analysis methods for detecting and characterising cone photoreceptors in diseased retinas. You will work with advanced retinal imaging datasets and collaborate closely with imaging researchers and ophthalmologists to investigate how cellular abnormalities relate to disease progression and patients' vision.
